claims.text: The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are crystalline solids with uniform elemental mixing.
Formation and growth of a metastable liquid-like surface layer govern the onset and progression of the phase transition.
Differential atomic mobilities among the constituent elements cause the liquid-like surface layer to form.
The liquid-like surface layer nucleates below the bulk melting point.
The surface layer is a precursor to full melting.
The nanoparticles will be heated under an inert atmosphere using a controlled temperature ramp across the premelting regime.
The tested temperature interval will span approximately 70% to 100% of the nominal bulk melting point.
Surface effects and surface diffusion are dominant in nanoparticles smaller than 50 nm.
Atoms at the nanoparticle surface become mobile at lower temperatures than atoms in the core.
Differences in constituent-element melting points contribute to the early surface mobility.
The metastable surface layer progressively thickens as temperature increases.
Progressive thickening of the liquid-like layer eventually produces homogeneous melting.
A disordered, liquid-like surface film will be observable before full melting.
The extent of the disordered surface film will increase with temperature.
The room-temperature baseline will show uniform crystallinity without surface disorder or liquid-like behavior.
The proposed surface-mediated mechanism is expected to dominate especially in nanoparticles below 50 nm under rapid heating.
The mechanism may not apply to larger bulk samples, where volume diffusion and homogeneous melting prevail.
Comparing slow and fast heating ramps will test whether surface-layer appearance and growth depend on heating rate.

Absence of localized surface disorder, a premelting DSC anomaly, and diffraction evidence of premelting, together with crystallinity loss only at the melting point, would falsify the proposed initiation mechanism.
